item.content:encoded:
El Wild Card de las Grandes Ligas arranca este martes 29 de septiembre con un duelo que promete encender los playoffs desde el primer lanzamiento: los New York Yankees reciben a los Boston Red Sox en Yankee Stadium, en una serie al mejor de tres juegos que representa una revancha directa de lo ocurrido el año pasado. El primer encuentro comenzará a las 20:00 horas del Este de Estados Unidos.
Hace un año, Yankees y Red Sox también se enfrentaron en el Wild Card y Nueva York terminó imponiéndose 2-1 en una serie que necesitó tres partidos. Ahora vuelven a encontrarse en el Bronx, con los Yankees como cuarto sembrado de la Liga Americana y Boston como quinto.
El Bronx vuelve a ser escenario de octubre
Nueva York tendrá la ventaja de disputar toda la serie como local. Uno de sus principales argumentos será Cam Schlittler, elegido para abrir el Juego 1 después de cerrar la temporada regular con marca de 14-6 y efectividad de 1.95.
El derecho ya sabe lo que significa enfrentar a Boston en octubre. En el Juego 3 del Wild Card de 2025 lanzó ocho entradas en blanco, ponchó a 12 bateadores y llevó a los Yankees a la siguiente ronda. Ahora volverá a recibir la pelota en el primer capítulo de una nueva batalla.
Del otro lado estará Payton Tolle, quien tendrá la responsabilidad de abrir por Boston. El joven lanzador tuvo buenos resultados frente a los Yankees durante la temporada y buscará darle a los Red Sox el primer golpe de la serie.
Aaron Judge, la gran incógnita
La principal duda para Nueva York está en su capitán. Aaron Judge continúa lidiando con una lesión en la pantorrilla y su disponibilidad para el primer encuentro permanece bajo evaluación.
La presencia del toletero sería un factor importante para la ofensiva de los Yankees, pero el equipo también se ha preparado para disputar la serie sin tenerlo disponible desde el inicio.
Boston, mientras tanto, llega con el recuerdo de la eliminación del año pasado y la posibilidad de cambiar la historia. No hay margen para una serie larga: el equipo que consiga dos victorias avanzará a la Serie Divisional contra Tampa Bay.
Dónde y cuándo ver
Yankees vs. Red Sox: martes 29 de septiembre
Transmisión: ESPN y Disney+
Hora: 18:00 horas, tiempo del centro de México
Estadio: Yankee Stadium
Formato: serie al mejor de tres

item.content:encoded:
For the 14th straight year, the Dodgers are postseason-bound.
Winners of three of the past six World Series, the Dodgers are looking to continue their reign. The back-to-back defending champions are bidding for the Major Leagues' first three-peat since the Yankees won three straight titles from 1998-2000.
The Dodgers, the No. 2 seed in the National League, are just about at full strength now that the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki have returned from the injured list, but there are several other compelling storylines to follow before the postseason.
Here's what to watch as the NL West-champion Dodgers forge their path back to the Fall Classic:
What could the postseason roster look like?
The strength of the Dodgers' pitching staff is the rotation, so expect them to carry more starters than they need and get creative with using some of them in relief. Manager Dave Roberts indicated that the team may carry only 12 pitchers to make room for an additional position player on the bench in the NL Division Series.
It may be premature to pencil in Josue De Paula, as the organization’s top prospect has played in only 11 big league games. But the Dodgers liked what they saw, and he could be an impact lefty bat off the bench.
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
First baseman (1): Freddie Freeman
Second baseman (1): Tommy Edman
Shortstop (1): Mookie Betts
Third baseman (1): Max Muncy
Outfielders (3): Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker
Utility/bench (3): Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim
Two-way player (1): Shohei Ohtani
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Relievers (9): Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Roki Sasaki, Kris Bubic, Brock Stewart
When does the postseason begin?
The NL Division Series begin on Saturday.
Who could be the Dodgers' NLDS opponent? 
The Dodgers won their 13th NL West title in the past 14 seasons and secured a first-round bye, so they will play the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and the Phillies.
Against which teams do the Dodgers have home-field advantage?
The Dodgers have home-field advantage over every team in the postseason field except the Brewers, who finished the regular season with the best record in the Majors.
What will the postseason rotation look like?
Yamamoto, Skubal, Snell and Glasnow make up this year's Big Four. The rotation order is yet to be determined. One consideration is that Yamamoto is accustomed to starting on at least five days' rest, whereas the other three are comfortable starting on four days' rest. That makes Yamamoto likely to start Game 1 of the NLDS because he would be available for a potential Game 5 on his normal rest. 
What's the latest on Ohtani's status?
Ohtani was activated from the 15-day IL and hit in the Dodgers' final five games, going 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts and one walk. Roberts described the performance as Ohtani showing some rust and said the team does not have any health concerns with him. 
Which injured players could return?   
The Dodgers hope that Henriquez, who has emerged as an important leverage arm, can return for the postseason after his regular season came to a premature end due to lower back discomfort. He will face hitters during the bye week, and as long as he comes away feeling good, he will be activated for the NLDS.
Which roster spots may be up for grabs?
The final spot on the bench is far from set in stone. The Dodgers could carry De Paula, but Dalton Rushing, Alex Call and Hyeseong Kim are additional options. This decision could come down to whether they want to use that bench spot on a potential impact bat or someone who brings enhanced speed and/or defense to the table. If L.A. carries fewer than 13 pitchers, that would open an additional bench spot.
The bullpen should also have some openings. If Henriquez does not recover in time for the postseason, that opens an additional spot. Justin Wrobleski, Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan were starters for most of the season, but they will be relief options in the postseason. But Wrobleski was inconsistent in the second half, and the Dodgers have other left-handers who may be more reliable in leverage, such as Bubic.
Who will close out games?
Díaz was supposed to resolve the Dodgers' ninth-inning troubles, but he has only added to them in his first year in L.A. Since returning from the IL, he has looked much better, which could have him back in the mix to close out games. The Dodgers may be more likely to play the matchups instead of going with a set closer in the postseason. Based on regular-season performance, Scott and Henriquez are two of the top options to pitch in save situations. Perhaps Sasaki could reprise his postseason closer role if needed.

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays entered 2026 expecting their offence to help carry them to another postseason run. Instead, a lineup that had been central to the club’s World Series appearance a year earlier became one of its biggest weaknesses. Established stars endured dramatic downturns, useful role players were asked to carry larger workloads and injuries forced Toronto to lean on several inexperienced hitters.
Anyone who watched the Blue Jays in 2026 knows they were not a good offensive team. They scored the fewest runs in all of baseball (648), hit the fewest home runs (152), and ranked second-worst in team OPS (.691) ahead of only the Los Angeles Angels.
There were still a few encouraging performances. But for every one of those successes they Blue Jays had another two or three hitters who fell short of expectations. The grades below weigh each hitter’s production against his role, opportunity and expectations entering the season.
Grading every Blue Jays hitter from the 2026 season
Alejandro Kirk
- HR: 10
- RBI: 43
- AVG: .278
- OPS: .767
- wRC+: 114
Kirk didn’t look like himself to start the year, then missed several months with a thumb injury. He recaptured his All-Star form when he finally returned, however, and led the Blue Jays offensively for much of the second half.
Grade: B+
Andrés Giménez
- HR: 9
- RBI: 59
- AVG: .244
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 81
Giménez is what he is at this point: a below-average hitter with a knack for coming through in the clutch. He still managed to accrue 2.8 fWAR on the strength of his stellar glovework at shortstop and contributions on the basepaths.
Grade: B-
Brandon Valenzuela
- HR: 9
- RBI: 24
- AVG: .226
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 96
Valenzuela filled in admirably for Kirk while he was on the injured list during the first half of the season. He flashed legitimate power upside at the plate before going ice-cold after the All-Star break, exposing the current limitations of his offensive profile.
Grade: C
Brett Bateman
- HR: 2
- RBI: 11
- AVG: .329
- OPS: .826
- wRC+: 138
Bateman exceeded all expectations after being acquired for Kevin Gausman at the trade deadline. He injected some life into the lineup immediately upon arrival and has likely cemented himself as a marquee piece of the 2027 squad.
Grade: A+
Charles McAdoo
- HR: 3
- RBI: 14
- AVG: .258
- OPS: .694
- wRC+: 93
McAdoo largely held his own at the plate with the Blue Jays in 2026. His approach needs work, but his combination of power and speed is exciting. He should keep improving with additional reps against MLB pitching.
Grade: C+
Davis Schneider
- HR: 5
- RBI: 16
- AVG: .145
- OPS: .624
- wRC+: 84
Schneider was one of several surprise contributors who propelled the Blue Jays to the World Series in 2025. His production fell off a cliff this year, which led to multiple demotions to Triple-A Buffalo. He might be out of runway.
Grade: F
Ernie Clement
- HR: 9
- RBI: 48
- AVG: .259
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 80
It was a tale of two seasons for Clement. He rode a strong first half to his first career All-Star appearance, then devolved into one of baseball’s worst hitters from August onward. He ended the year with the worst offensive numbers of his career.
Grade: C-
George Springer
- HR: 15
- RBI: 54
- AVG: .249
- OPS: .726
- wRC+: 105
Springer redeemed what was likely his final season with the Blue Jays with a strong second half. While he didn’t come anywhere near his 2025 numbers, he still put together a solid season. His contract was worth every penny.
Grade: B-
Jésus Sánchez
- HR: 8
- RBI: 35
- AVG: .254
- OPS: .713
- wRC+: 99
He makes the list because he was on the team for most of the year before being designated for assignment in September. He failed to turn his power potential into actual production, and the less that can be said about his defence, the better.
Grade: D
Josh Smith
- HR: 6
- RBI: 15
- AVG: .203
- OPS: .611
- wRC+: 75
Smith was a pleasant surprise down the stretch after coming over in the Adam Macko trade, hitting five of his six home runs after coming to Toronto. He should have an opportunity to compete for a bench spot on the 2027 squad.
Grade: B-
Kazuma Okamoto
- HR: 33
- RBI: 92
- AVG: .232
- OPS: .762
- wRC+: 113
The general consensus on Okamoto coming over from Japan was that he would hit for a high average with some power. He ended up being more of a three true outcome guy who led the team in home runs, RBI, and strikeouts by a wide margin.
Grade: B+
Myles Straw
- HR: 3
- RBI: 26
- AVG: .241
- OPS: .646
- wRC+: 83
Straw wound up getting far more plate appearances than anyone expected he would coming into the year. Unsurprisingly, he didn’t do much with those opportunities. His value is in his speed, excellent defensive play, and clubhouse presence.
Grade: C+
Nathan Lukes:
- HR: 10
- RBI: 41
- AVG: .277
- OPS: .725
- wRC+: 102
Lukes got off to an extremely rough start at the plate while managing a bout of vertigo, but eventually settled back into his usual form. He’s a league-average hitter who grinds out at-bats—a quintessentially glue guy in a deeper lineup.
Grade: B
Sean Keys
- HR: 2
- RBI: 9
- AVG: .197
- OPS: .570
- wRC+: 57
Assigning Keys a letter grade almost feels unfair given how little he played. Still, he flashed some power potential in his limited opportunities, albeit while appearing generally overmatched by major league pitching. He’s very much a work in progress.
Grade: C
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
- HR: 9
- RBI: 57
- AVG: .260
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 95
This might be the most disappointing season by a hitter in the 50-year history of the franchise. Coming off a historic postseason, Guerrero authored one of the most pathetic performances by a superstar in recent memory. That ridiculous quote didn’t help, either.
Grade: F

item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to this season’s final edition of Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
TUESDAY
With his 25th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing broke Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
Kodai Senga became one of just 11 Japanese-born players to reach eight career saves, joining: Kazuhiro Sasaki (129), Koji Uehara (95), Takashi Saito (84), Akinori Otsuka (39), Shigetoshi Hasegawa (33), Shingo Takatsu (27), Hideki Irabu (16), Hisanori Takahashi (10), Masanori Murakami (9), and Yoshihisa Hirano (8).
Francisco Alvarez and Carson Benge each hit two doubles, marking the first time multiple Mets hit multiple doubles in a game since Ronny Mauricio and Jeff McNeil did it on July 27, 2025, in San Francisco.
WEDNESDAY
Marcus Semien hit his 15th home run of the year, giving the Mets six or more players with 15+ homers for the fifth time in franchise history after 2000 (7), 2017 (8), 2019 (6), and 2025 (6). The only teams with more 15-homer players this season were the Cubs, Reds, and Dodgers (all tied at 7). Of the Mets’ players with 15+ homers last season and this season, only two (Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto) overlap.
Juan Soto reached base four times for the 103rd time in his career, moving past Ted Williams for the third-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Mickey Mantle (121) and Jimmie Foxx (112).
Soto became the fifth Met to get intentionally walked three times in a game, after Claudell Washington (August 26, 1980), Vince Coleman (August 10, 1992), Todd Hundley (June 28, 1997), and David Wright (May 19, 2007, and July 18, 2009).
Brett Baty’s 455-foot home run tied the longest blast of his big league career, a homer off Brad Lord on August 20, 2025, in Washington.
Francisco Alvarez’s seventh-inning single registered an exit velocity of 113.7 mph. It was Alvarez’s 15th career batted ball with an exit velocity of 112+ mph, the second-most by a Met player in the Statcast era (since 2015) behind Pete Alonso, who had a whopping 130.
Alvarez, Lindor, and Baty each recorded a batted ball with an exit velocity over 110 mph, marking the first time the Mets recorded three batted balls with an exit velocity of 110+ mph in the same game since September 10, 2025, in Philadelphia.
Nolan McLean completed his rookie year with a total of 179.2 innings pitched, the most by a Mets rookie since Jae Weong Seo (188.1 in 2003), and 194 strikeouts, the third-most by a Mets rookie behind Dwight Gooden (276 in 1984) and Kodai Senga (202 in 2023).
McLean recorded his 250th strikeout in his 39th career game, tying Jacob deGrom for the fifth-fewest games by a Met to reach that milestone behind Dwight Gooden (29 games), Matt Harvey (34 games), Noah Syndergaard (36 games), and Kodai Senga (38 games).
McLean recorded his 26th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since deGrom (29) and Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
McLean became the first rookie with 20 quality starts since the Royals’ Yordano Ventura (22 in 2014). McLean’s 20 quality starts this season were tied with Sonny Gray and Cam Schlittler for fifth-most in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (22), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (22), Sandy Alcantara (21), and Michael Wacha (21). McLean also recorded his 21st start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
THURSDAY
Zac Thornton’s 63 strikeouts through 15 career games ranks fourth among Mets left-handers, behind Steven Matz (87), Bill Pulsipher (74), and David Peterson (69).
Juan Soto became the second Mets player to get intentionally walked four times in a two-game span, after Travis d’Arnaud did it while batting in the No. 8 spot ahead of Jon Niese and Bartolo Colón on June 1-2, 2014, in Philadelphia.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 63rd time this season. That ties 2013 for the most such games the Mets have had in a season in the Wild-Card Era (since 1995).
Over the franchise’s first five trips to Arlington, the Mets are still yet to lose a series on the road against the Rangers. They won two of three in 2003, won two of three in 2011, split a two-game set in 2017, won two out of three in 2024, and won two out of three again in 2026.
FRIDAY
Carson Benge became the first Mets rookie with 20+ homers and 20+ stolen bases in a season.
Benge became just the eighth player in MLB history to join the 20/20 club in their debut season, joining: Jackson Chourio (2024), Anthony Volpe (2023), Bobby Witt Jr. (2022), Julio Rodríguez (2022), Marty Cordova (1995), Ellis Burks (1987), and Mitchell Page (1977). (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Benge recorded his 43rd multi-hit game of the season, breaking Pete Alonso’s 2019 record for the most multi-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
With a pinch-hit single in the eighth inning, Brett Baty extended his career-high 18-game on-base streak. It was snapped with an 0-for-4 performance on Saturday.
Bo Bichette hit his fourth home run at Nationals Park this season, tied for the most by a Mets player in any season on the road against the Nats/Expos. His six extra-base hits trail only David Wright (7) in 2012.
Francisco Lindor didn’t notch his 300th home run on Friday night, but he did record three batted balls in a game at 107+ mph for the first time in the Statcast era (since 2015). Unfortunately for him, only one of the three resulted in a base hit.
The Mets allowed five wild pitches in a game and four wild pitches in an inning for the first time in franchise history.
SATURDAY
Jonah Tong set career highs with nine strikeouts and 19 whiffs in a game.
Mets pitchers recorded 14 or more strikeouts in a game for the 12th time this season, the fourth-most such games in a season in franchise history behind 2021 (19), 2019 (17), and 2022 (17).
With a start at shortstop, Brett Baty became the first Mets player to play six different positions in a season since Jeff McNeil in 2023.
Nate Lavender has recorded 19 scoreless appearances in his first 21 career outings, tied with Jaime Cerda, Erik Goeddel, and Daniel Zamora for the second-most by a Met behind Joe Smith (20).
In the Mets’ penultimate game of the season, their No. 8 and No. 9 hitters hit back-to-back homers (A.J. Ewing and Ronny Mauricio). The 2026 Mets had done that once before — in their first game of the season, when Carson Benge and Francisco Alvarez went deep at Citi Field against the Pirates.
The Mets clinched their sixth consecutive victory in the season series with Washington. Their record against the Nationals is 57-33 over that span.
SUNDAY
Francisco Lindor became the fifth player to hit their 300th career home run while having played at least 50% of their games at shortstop, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Tejada. (source: Sarah Langs on X) He is also the 11th switch-hitter to reach the 300-homer mark. (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Lindor became one of 27 players with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, and the third active player to have reached the milestone along with Andrew McCutchen and Mike Trout. He is the fifth member of that club to have played for the Mets; the others were Willie Mays, Darryl Strawberry, Gary Sheffield, and Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor became the seventh player to hit their 300th home run as a Met, joining Dave Kingman, George Foster, Gary Carter, Mike Piazza, Mo Vaughn, and Curtis Granderson.
Lindor’s 300th homer registered a 110.8-mph exit velocity, marking the third-hardest-hit homer as a right-handed batter in his career. His only harder-hit homer from the right side as a Met came on another afternoon in Washington, when he took MacKenzie Gore deep on August 21, 2025.
Ronny Maurcio became the first Met to hit three consecutive homers out of the No. 9 spot, with two on Saturday and one on Sunday. (source: SNY broadcast)
Carson Benge recorded his 14th three-hit game of the season, extending his record for the most three-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
Juan Soto holds a 1.101 OPS against the Nationals in 39 games played facing his former team. That’s the third-highest OPS for any player with at least 150 plate appearances against the Nationals/Expos, trailing only Jim Edmonds (1.198) and Todd Helton (1.114).
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Let’s talk about the rookies.
In Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing, and Zac Thornton, the Mets have four rookies with at least 1.5 bWAR*. That’s tied for the most rookies with 1.5+ bWAR* in a season in franchise history, matching the mark from 1983 (Darryl Strawberry, Carlos Diaz, Walt Terrell, and Doug Sisk).
In Benge, McLean, and Ewing, the Mets have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*. Prior to this year, they had never had as many as two such rookies in a single season. In fact, the 2026 Mets are just the third team in the modern era (since 1900) to have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*, joining:
2006 Marlins (4: Hanley Ramírez, Dan Uggla, Josh Johnson, and Aníbal Sánchez)
1989 Orioles (3: Randy Milligan, Bob Milacki, Gregg Olson)
*bWAR separated for position players and pitchers, not cumulative
Thank you for following along all year! Here’s to many more stat parties in 2027…

It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins.
New York seems to awaken something within the Polar Bear. After hitting his 300th career homer back at Citi Field on Sept. 15, Alonso needed just eight more games to notch No. 307 – a jaw-dropping 471 foot shot – in a two-homer performance at Yankee Stadium on Friday night. Over his last five games in Toronto and the Bronx, Alonso reached base in 11 of his 22 plate appearances, recording five homers, eight RBIs and eight runs scored. The effort earned the first baseman his second Player of the Week Award of the second half.
Even with the Orioles’ final game of the season cancelled due to inclement weather, Alonso outpaced Yordan Alvarez to lead the American League in homers (43) and RBIs (113). He previously led the National League in RBIs with the Mets in 2022 (131), making him the first player in Major League history to lead both leagues in RBIs. He also played in every one of his team’s games for a third consecutive season.
The D-backs couldn’t complete their bid for the third NL Wild Card spot, but their veteran third baseman did just about everything he could to will them there. A game after hitting a go-ahead grand slam against the Yankees on Sept. 21, he finished a triple shy of the cycle at Coors Field on Tuesday to commence the ninth Player of the Week campaign of his career. Over the Snakes’ final six games in Colorado and San Diego, Arenado went 10-for-23 (.435) with three homers, two doubles and 5 RBIs.
With a two-run home run in San Diego on Friday, the 35-year-old notched his eighth 30-homer season and his first since 2022 with the Cardinals. The only players with more 30-homer seasons as primary third basemen are Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12) and Eddie Mathews (10).
Acuña has a complicated history with the loanDepot park outfield. This March, he clinched a World Baseball Classic championship there with Team Venezuela; but in July 2021, the right fielder tore his right ACL while leaping for a ball near the fence, sidelining him for the remainder of the Braves’ World Series campaign. On Saturday afternoon, less than 72 hours before kicking off a run at another title, Acuña proved he truly has no fear of the Miami warning track.
With no outs and a runner on first in the opening frame, Marlins slugger Heriberto Hernández lofted a Brent Suter sinker the opposite way at 101.2 mph. Acuña darted to his right at 25.6 feet per second, leapt at the fence and went tumbling to the dirt with the ball secured, giving the Braves a loud first out of the game. (Hernández went on to record his 25th homer the next day, wisely pulling the ball to left field rather than testing Acuña again.)

MILWAUKEE — Team captains are not common in Major League Baseball. But on Saturday, the Milwaukee Brewers named Christian Yelich the first captain in franchise history, making him one of only three active captains in the majors.
The Brewers decided in a team meeting prior to its Saturday game against the St. Louis Cardinals to give the honor to Yelich. But Yelich did not want to accept without “sign-off” from another Brewers legend: Robin Yount.
Yelich requested that Yount, who played his entire 20-year career with Milwaukee, sign off on his captaincy before accepting. Yount, a Hall of Famer, was a leader on the only Brewers’ team to make the World Series in 1982.
Yount joined Wisconsin’s Midday News to discuss the conversations he had with Yelich and Brewers Manager Pat Murphy ahead of Saturday’s announcement.
“In all honesty, they certainly didn’t need my approval,” Yount said. “But in saying that, it was very, very humbling to be honest, to think that they would even consider asking me what I thought.”
Yount said the fact that he was asked speaks to the character of this team, calling them a “class act, especially at this time of the season.”
While Yount has not been around the current Brewers team as much as in previous years, he said he got to know Yelich through their mutual friend, Bob Uecker.
“I learned a lot about Christian through the years Ueck was around him,” Yount said. “Ueck spoke of Christian in the highest regard… The team pretty much looked up to him as that guy. And that’s all I needed to hear from somebody that was around him enough.”

He was traded (via the Toronto Blue Jays) earlier this year.

Looking At Gausman’s Other Stops
Gausman was picked in the 1st round of the 2012 MLB Draft.
He is in the middle of his 14th season at the MLB level.
In addition to the Cubs and Blue Jays, Gausman has also had stops with the Baltimore Orioles, San Francisco Giants, Atlanta Braves and Cincinnati Reds.
Gausman is a two-time MLB All-Star.
He has gone 121-125 with a 3.87 ERA in 393 career games (354 starts).
Looking At The Cubs
The Cubs finished the regular season with an 89-73 record.
They were the second-place team in the National League Central.

item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

As the 2026 MLB postseason prepares to begin, it's a good time for some bold predictions about who will win and why, from the wild-card rounds to the World Series.
Chicago White Sox at Houston Astros
Houston was just 11-13 in September and it felt like neither the Astros nor the Texas Rangers wanted to win the AL West. Houston finally did on the last day, but the Astros aren't inspiring confidence that they can go deep into the postseason.
The White Sox could have been the AL Central champs, but couldn't hang on as Cleveland made a hard charge and overtook them. For a team that has been told all season about they are still living in the shadow of a 121-loss season two years ago, this team has a chip on its shoulder. That should push the White Sox into the next round.
Boston Red Sox at New York Yankees
After a chaotic weather weekend in the Northeast that forced the Red Sox to play Game 162 in Tampa and canceled the final game of the season for the Yankees, that extra day of rest (and far less travel) may help New York when the wild-card series opens in the Bronx.
New York's pitching lineup of Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole will be enough to overcome any of the Yankees' offensive issues in a series that will last just two games.
Philadelphia Phillies at Atlanta Braves
Like Houston, Philadelphia did little to inspire confidence in its postseason future at the end of the regular season. It's also been a season where the Braves have Philadelphia's number, winning nine of the 13 games the two rivals have played. Atlanta sweeps Philadelphia.
Chicago Cubs at San Diego Padres
The Padres are red-hot entering the wild card, going 18-6 in September to secure a home series. Having the home fans on their side, San Diego will continue its solid play by sweeping the Cubs into the offseason.
New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays
While the Yankees may have had enough to get into the ALDS, there's little doubt that the Rays are the better team.
All season, it was a question of if New York could catch Tampa Bay for the AL East title. The Rays kept showing they weren't going to crack under any pressure, and that continues with a 3-1 series win to move on to the ALCS.
Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians
Chicago's story has been incredible, but there's a reason why the Guardians won the division ... and keep a reputation as the team that doesn't die easily. They're built for pressure and the postseason and will dispatch the White Sox in four games.
Atlanta Braves vs. Los Angeles Dodgers
This will be must-see TV as two of the NL's behemoths battle it out. The home advantage will make a difference for the Dodgers, who will win in Game 5 to seal another trip to the NLCS.
San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers
Milwaukee is for real. There have been plenty of instances in the past where the Brewers have stumbled in the postseason, but this won't be a repeat of those mistakes. Jacob Misiorowski will set the tone in the first game and the Brewers will win in four.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Cleveland Guardians
The Rays went 5-1 against Cleveland this season. With homefield advantage, there's no reason to think that trend won't continue. Look for the Rays to oust the Guardians in six games.
Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Milwaukee Brewers
This season, the Brewers are 4-3 against the Dodgers. With Milwaukee holding home-field advantage, this is the year that Los Angeles is finally stopped short of winning it all.
There is a lot to like for Milwaukee in their relief pitching options, and it may come down to that. While the Dodgers may have the better rotation, Milwaukee has the better pitching staff overall. Pitching wins in October, and the Brewers win a classic in seven games in front of their home fans.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers
A World Series without a "major market" in it? Oh this will set up plenty of conversations for what will be a contentious offseason.
Neither of these teams have won a World Series, making for another fascinating storyline in what will be an epic Fall Classic. Milwaukee has the home-field advantage thanks to their 103 regular-season wins, and that makes a big difference in this battle of the top seeds.
Brewers in six.

Since 1950, there have only been four pitchers to lead the league in ERA, strikeouts, and opponents' batting average.
Here in 2026, Milwaukee Brewers' ace Jacob Misiorowski officially joined that list.
Misiorowski now finds himself in the same conversation as Sandy Koufax (1965), J.R. Richard (1979), and Mike Scott (1986), according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Brewers' regular season ended the exact same way it started, and that was with Misiorowski picking up a win.
His 16th win of the year was a nearly flawless 5.1-inning performance, one that proved this 24-year-old has what it takes to help the Brewers make a deep run in the postseason.
Misiorowski caps off historic 2026 season
Going back 76 years, Miz joins an exclusive club that features a few all-time greats. To think this accomplishment hasn't been done since 1986 is even more incredible, especially knowing how many stellar pitchers have won the Cy Young and taken the world by storm since then.
Misiorowski made 30 starts this season as he posted league-best numbers in strikeouts (252), ERA (1.80), and opponents' batting average (.157).
Those obviously aren't the only statistics that he led the league in, but those are the three that helped him make history dating back to 1950.
Misiorowski's speed is unheard of
For a starting pitcher to be able to throw 100+ miles per hour consistently is something that isn't seen too often in the modern era.
Sure, having a closer come in and throw that is one thing, but to see Misiorowski do it as consistently as he did was another.
Officially, his 1,115 pitches at 100+ mph this season were the most since tracking started in 2008. Previously, the record was set by Jordan Hicks in 2018, but he only threw 673 that year.
To say "only" in that sentence proves just how out-of-this-world Misiorowski's stuff truly is.
His regular season came to an end with 174.2 innings thrown, so that comes out to roughly 6.4 pitches of 100+ mph thrown per inning.
Brewers are hungry for a World Series
Keep in mind, Misiorowski appeared out of the bullpen in three postseason games a year ago. He was 2-1 and sported a 1.50 ERA and 0.83 WHIP in his 12 innings pitched.
Misiorowski had a 5.3 K/BB ratio in a limited sample size last year, so it's incredible to think that number was 5.7 here in the regular season.
If there's anyone who can help guide the Brewers to a World Series, it's Misiorowski, and now he gets some much-needed rest as this team went 103-59 and is able to skip the Wild Card round for the second straight season.

NEW YORK -- Who could forget the tone that Garrett Crochet set at Yankee Stadium in Game 1 of last year’s American League Wild Card Series, when he turned in a masterful performance which included 11 strikeouts over 7 2/3 innings and 117 pitches?
But the fact that Crochet’s even here, and in very much in play to be added to the roster as a reliever when it is announced on Tuesday, is satisfying to the lefty who finished second in the AL Cy Young Award race last season.
This season was a rough letdown, filled with left shoulder woes, a setback, and ultimately months of strengthening and rehabbing the capsule that surrounds his rotator cuff just so he could be cleared to throw again.
On Saturday, in Fort Myers, Fla., he threw his second live batting practice session of the week.
“It was good. Been feeling good. I guess now it's just a matter if anybody agrees with me,” said Crochet.
“We're still seeing,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “Again, like I said, he threw the live BP and came out of it well. We'll see as we get to the end of the workout if we can key down on making decisions like that.”
One key question is if Crochet will be able to pitch more than once against the Yankees, which feels important in a best-of-three format.
“I think the answer to that is up in the air,” said Tracy. “If we're able to activate Garrett and we do that and we decide to do that, obviously he's available, right? I think beyond that, if you were to use him, the availability, whether that's the next day or for another game in the Series, it's still going to be contingent on us continuing to evaluate him.
“We know where he's at. We know he's worked very hard to get everything back strong the way it needs to be, but we're still going to be evaluating him daily to see where he's at. Whether he's available to pitch [more than once] in this series, I don't know the answer to that yet.”
For months, Crochet was frustrated by a rehab that turned out to be longer than he ever envisioned. But he didn’t let that frustration diminish his motivation to put himself in position to be part of Boston’s playoff run.
“It was obviously a lot longer than I expected. Been busting my tail just to kind of give myself a fighting chance, and I feel like I did that,” said Crochet. “Now it's just waiting for the roster to come out. I hope that I'm able to contribute, but regardless, I'm here, and I think that we have put ourselves in a great position to walk away from the Series with a win.”
Last year, Crochet got the only win of the series for the Red Sox. This year, Boston looks for a chance to get rivalry redemption.
Will that experience in Game 1 last year help him if he gets the chance to face the Yankees again this week?
“It's more so just awareness of being in the moment of the postseason and being able to quiet the noise on the outside, just not letting the moment get too big,” Crochet said.
Pitching in relief is familiar for Crochet. He did it in college at Tennessee and in his first 72 career appearances (2.71 ERA) for the White Sox before he was converted to a starting pitcher in ‘24.
Considering that Crochet hasn’t had time to stretch out his pitch count, one or two-inning stints seem most likely should he make the roster.
